Has the Department of Veterans Affairs or the Canadian pension commission received a brief from the dominion council of War Amputations of Canada requesting a reassessment of the Symes pension and, if so, is consideration being given to implementing the recommendations contained therein?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The minister received representation from the War Amputations of Canada by way of a brief submitted early in 1962. Because the representation asked that the commission introduce certain amendments to the table of disabilities affecting assessments for Symes operations, the matter was referred to the pension commission for consideration. The representation was carefully considered at a general meeting of the commission on April 17, 1962. The War Amputations of Canada were advised of the commission's decision by letter from the chairman on May 11, 1962.
While the decision at that time was adverse, this matter is to be further considered at a general meeting of the Canadian pension commission early in 1963.

1.	Who Investigated the possibilities offered by Mont Tremblant, In Terrebonne county, Que., before Banff, Alta, was given priority for the coming Olympic games?
2.	Was a written report submitted and, if so, is it a public document?
3.	Why was Mont Tremblant not selected as the site for the winter Olympics?

1 and 3. On January 9, 1961, the Canadian Olympic association commissioned the Foundation of Canada Engineering Corporation Limited to carry out a comparative site study of various

centres which were interested in making application for the holding of the 1968 winter Olympic games.
Prior to this the Canadian Olympic association had given notification through the newspapers that it would consider applications from sites interested in holding the games. Applications were received from the Calgary Olympic development association representing Banff, the Snow Valley Olympic winter Olympic committee representing Fernie, B.C., the Rossland-Trail Olympic committee representing Rossland, B.C., the Manning Park Olympic committee representing Manning Park, B.C., the Garibaldi Olympic development association representing Alta Lake, B.C., and the Revelstoke winter Olympic games committee representing Revelstoke, B.C. No representation was made to the Canadian Olympic association on behalf of Mont Tremblant.
As a result of this survey Banff was recommended to the Canadian Olympic association as the most suitable site. It is understood that only the locations in Canada which could meet specifications for Olympic competition in ski events are those in the Rocky mountains.
2. Yes, a report was submitted by the Foundation of Canada Engineering Corporation Limited to the Canadian Olympic association. A copy is on the files of the Department of National Health and Welfare.

1.	How many cases, to date, of polio have been reported in Canada following administration of Sabin vaccine?
2.	Has the Sabin vaccine program been completely cancelled in Canada and, if not, is there any indication when the Sabin vaccine program may be resumed?

1. As indicated in the statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare in the House of Commons on November 14, in approximately four million persons fed Sabin vaccine in May, June and July, there were four cases of paralytic disease with a high probability of association with Sabin vaccine. Among the contacts of those fed Sabin vaccine, one case of paralytic poliomyelitis was considered by the national technical advisory committee on live poliovirus vaccines to have a high probability of association with Sabin vaccine.
2. As indicated in the minister's statement of November 14, he has accepted the recommendation of the dominion council of health that the use of Sabin vaccine be deferred no longer and that it be used according to the recommendations of the national technical
Questions
advisory committee on live poliovirus vaccines. Specific plans regarding the use of Sabin vaccine will be determined by provincial departments of health.

subsubtopic: UNDERDEVELOPED NATIONS
speechtext: Has the United Nations or any agency thereof or any nation or private organization advanced proposals for the promotion of private investment in, or subscription to, a fund to be administered by the United Nations, to be used for assistance to underdeveloped nations?

subsubtopic: UNDERDEVELOPED NATIONS
speechtext:
No. Mr. Speaker, I do not have any knowledge of any formal proposals to promote the development of a specific private subscription fund to be administered by the United Nations on behalf of the less developed countries. However, it is a fact that private individuals and groups in a number of countries, including Canada, do contribute privately to the work of the United Nations.
Under the financial regulations of the United Nations, voluntary contributions from non-governmental sources may be accepted by the secretary general for purposes consistent with the policies, aims and objectives of the organization. Moneys accepted for purposes specified, or reasonably indicated, by the donor are treated as trust funds or special accounts and are used to augment the work of the organization by allocation to projects or programs in respect of which the use of extra-budgetary funds is proper. However, moneys accepted in respect of which no purpose is specified or indicated are treated as miscellaneous income which is used merely to reduce the assessments that would otherwise be payable by all member states, not solely the assessment of the donors' country.
The usual practice, and it is one which is encouraged by the United Nations, is for private donors to specify the particular program to be assisted by their contributions. Chief among these are the expanded program for technical assistance, the special fund, the fund for the Congo, the high commissioner for refugees and the international children's emergency fund, UNICEF.
It is, of course, also possible to make private contributions in a similar fashion to the work of one or other of the specialized agencies and of the international atomic agency.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I beg leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the need to provide parliament with full information on the current conflict between the board of broadcast governors and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, which threatens to deprive the public of national coverage of the Grey cup game. Before Your Honour rules on the matter I ask that leave be given to me to argue the case, if I may.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I trust that the hon. member will be arguing his case as to urgency of debate, not as to the subject matter of the motion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: If Your Honour wishes me to deal with that question first I shall be glad to do so. As Your Honour knows under standing order 26 and the citations as laid down in Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 100, the manner in which standing order 26 is interpreted is set out. The first point is that the matter must involve the administrative responsibility of the government; and I do not intend to deal with that point unless Your Honour suggests that I should do so. However, the next one indicates that the matter must be pressing in the public interest; and third is the urgency of debate. Your Honour has suggested that I might address myself to that part of the citation, and I do so.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: That is the first point. I should like to hear argument first on the basis of the urgency of debate; then we shall go into the matter of urgent importance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
On the question of urgency of debate may I say this. Your Honour is aware of the list of business given by the house leader on Thursday. It is quite a lengthy list, and it was repeated in part on Friday. During the whole of this week certainly there will be no opportunity to discuss a matter of this nature.
Motion for Adjournment
Then again, speaking on the merits of the case, I think in his answer to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickers-gill) the minister clearly indicated the urgency of the matter, which in a nutshell is this, namely that there has been a ruling by the B.B.G. ordering the C.B.C., under certain penalties, to broadcast the Grey cup game.
I have the order here, if Your Honour wishes me to refer to it. Section 16 (2) of the regulations is amended to read as follows:
AH stations shall broadcast the program referred to in subsection (1) -
And the program referred to therein is the 1962 football game.
-in its entirety and shall not omit or increase any portion of the entertainment or advertising content of the program.
Then there is the decision taken by the C.B.C. over the week end which is in violation of that order, because it says that it will broadcast the game but not including the commercials. Hence there is a complete contradiction between the regulatory body and the crown corporation for which the minister is responsible in this house. I am not saying that there is an obligation on the government to determine the issue, but I am saying that there is an obligation on the government to provide information to this house with reference to the subject matter. Under these three heads I think there is established a case for urgency of debate. There is also the matter of the administrative responsibility of the government to be considered. As I said earlier, here are two bodies, one a crown corporation and the other the regulating body.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order. While the hon. gentleman is addressing the Chair, I wish the Chair could hear him. There seems to be an undercurrent of comment-I do not know whether private conferences are going on-which makes it rather difficult for the Chair and the other hon. members of the house to hear what is being said.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I was going on to say, Mr. Speaker, that there is an administrative responsibility on the part of the government. Here are two bodies, one a crown corporation and the other a regulatory body, both of which are responsible to parliament through the minister who is the channel of communication in this case.
I say this to the minister without the slightest disrespect. Until today there has been no attempt to answer questions which have been put orally on the orders of the day or which have been placed on the order paper. Perhaps I should put it this way, that the minister

Motion for Adjournment lias been reluctant in giving information to the house under the circumstances save and except the information which was given today.
The third prerequisite has to do with the matter of immediate attention or, to use the words here, the matter "must be so pressing that public interest will suffer if it is not given immediate attention". Everyone knows that the game will take place next Saturday.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Just listen carefully to what I have said. I have made no mistake. 1 did not say "this Saturday"; I said "next Saturday".

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I was interrupted by the Prime Minister who-

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: No interruption at all; not the slightest.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I thought he had interrupted me.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is addressing the Chair on the point of urgency of debate, and I do not think it should be within this discussion to encourage intervention from other members, so if he will address himself to the Chair we will proceed.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
To satisfy those who interrupted me a moment ago I will give the date and then there will be no difficulty. It is December 1. But meanwhile there is a cleavage, an impasse between these two bodies on the one hand, and there is an urgency to determine the issue between the two. The government seems to be doing nothing through its ordinary channel of communication, namely the minister, to dispose of the matter.
Therefore I submit to you with deference, Mr. Speaker, that under these three heads the house should be allowed to discuss the merits of the case so that we may put certain questions to the minister and be enabled to obtain from him information which the house is entitled to have under these circumstances, but which the house has been prevented from getting. Under these circumstances, sir, I believe I am entitled to proceed with the motion as submitted.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has laboured hard and most ineffectively to try to establish urgency of debate in relation to this matter. Mr. Speaker, what is it that he wishes to debate? If you will examine the motion you will see that he wishes to debate the current conflict, as he describes it, between these two bodies. He wishes to discuss a matter of urgent public importance,


namely the need to provide parliament with full information on what he calls the current conflict between two public bodies. It is not the matter of the holding of the game or the broadcasting of the game, but rather this question of conflict that he wishes to discuss.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Read the whole motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Even if he had been right in assuming that the game was being played on Saturday of this week instead of on December 1-and this explains, of course, a good deal of his error in regard to the matter of urgency-even if the game was being played this week there still would not be a matter here of urgency of debate at all, because it is the question of the conflict that he wishes to discuss. As the hon. member has indicated, it is not a question of broadcasting the game because he himself has said that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has said that it is willing to broadcast the game less the commercials. Therefore no question as to the public seeing the game is involved here.
Lastly, Mr. Speaker, there is the very clear point that here we are dealing with what is described by the hon. member as a conflict between two public bodies set up by parliament, neither of which falls within the administrative responsibility of the government. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, on all these grounds I submit that here is no urgency of debate within the established rules of the house.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words in support of the hon. member for Laurier on the urgency of having the subject matter of this motion discussed by parliament. If, as the Minister of Justice says, these two bodies are not responsible to the government, then certainly they are responsible to this parliament, and this parliament should have the opportunity to discuss the manner in which they are conducting the important affairs of broadcasting in this country.
Discussion of this conflict is urgent on three grounds. The first is that members have a right to the opportunity to discuss whether the order issued by the board of broadcast governors was valid and legal. Second, members should have the opportunity to discuss the possibility that the board of broadcast governors may take the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to court, and surely this is something which ought to be discussed quite soon. The whole country is perturbed about this conflict between two public bodies, and many people who are in favour of publicly owned and publicly sponsored broadcasting are convinced that the Canadian Broadcasting

Corporation is being undermined. I think parliament should have the opportunity to see whether or not that is true.
I point out further that since the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has indicated that it will carry the game but not the advertising, there is a distinct possibility that the private network may refuse to pass on the game to the C.B.C., and this would mean that areas in Canada which are served solely by the C.B.C. would not be able to see the game. Surely this question ought to be resolved not the day before the game, but quickly, and it cannot be resolved quickly if these two bodies cannot be brought together. Apparently the government has done nothing in this direction, and surely parliament should have the opportunity to discuss this matter and to issue an order to these bodies which in the final analysis are responsible to this House of Commons.
(Translation):

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am surprised to note that a football game is dealt with as if it were an urgent matter. When my friend the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dumont) asked that the problem of farmers be considered as an urgent matter, not one Liberal member agreed to support him.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Completely outside the question.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the adjournment of the house could have been moved to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely the unemployment problem. We have nothing against the fact that the house is discussing that football game, but since we shall not be playing football and handling television cameras on that day, what can we do about it?
In my opinion, the house should ask the Secretary of State (Mr. Halpenny), who answers for those two organizations, to suggest that they agree on the principles that would guide their decision concerning the broadcasting of that football game which the Canadian people would like to see on television.
That is what the house should ask the Secretary of State to do. I am of the opinion that it is not urgent to discuss this question today.

speakeroldname: Mr. R. J. McCleave (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I draw the attention of the house to a new facet of the argument. I understand that the board of broadcast governors is meeting today to deal with this very problem, and if I am correct in that information I would draw Your Honour's
Motion for Adjournment attention to Beauchesne, page 92, where it is said that the Speaker must "enforce the principle that subjects excluded by those rules cannot be brought forward thereon"- that is on such as the motion proposed this afternoon-"such as a matter under adjudication by a court of law, or matters already discussed or appointed for consideration during the current session", and so on.
The point I make is based on the analogy that the board of broadcast governors has been vested by parliament with at least quasi-judicial powers. It is seized of this very problem not at some future time but this afternoon. Therefore I suggest it would be presumptuous for us, having given that problem to the board, now to take it back for debate here at least until they have concluded their discussions.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. W. Baldwin (Parliamentary Secretary io fhe Prime Minisler):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Laurier has already referred to citation 100 in Beauchesne. I would take you forward to section 8 under that citation, on page 91, where there is the following:
What I think was contemplated, was an occurrence of some sudden emergency, either in home or in foreign affairs.
I underline the words "sudden emergency".
This dispute has been the subject of a number of questions asked in this house over the past several weeks. I refer you, for example, to November 1, when there was a question asked by the hon. member for Port Arthur concerning the dispute between the C.B.C. and the B.B.G. over the coverage of this game. The B.B.G. was not mentioned, but this dispute was. In so far as the question of urgency is concerned, I may say there was a supply motion on November 5 when the opposition had every opportunity, if they so desired, to mention this subject as a grievance. They saw fit to deal with another matter, and I submit that takes care of the question of the urgency of debate.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I wish to deal with the matter of urgency of debate, and especially the arguments presented by my hon. friends opposite relating to this point. The Minister of Justice, in his comments, failed to deal with the essential point that has been raised on previous occasions, especially by Mr. Speaker Michener who unfailingly, in dealing with a matter of this kind, asked whether the subject matter anticipated a matter previously arranged for consideration by the house. Nothing that has been said from the other side indicates that this subject can be discussed on any other occasion. There is no item listed on the order paper, and there

Motion for Adjournment is no opportunity to deal with this matter. This is the point I should like to make in respect to the argument presented by the Minister of Justice.
I felt that the argument made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Public Works missed the point. The B.B.G. is not a court of law. The B.B.G. and the C.B.C. are public agencies operating under the parliament of Canada.
The parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister states that this particular rule No. 26 can only be used in case of a sudden emergency or a sudden development. I submit that the sudden emergency or sudden development did occur on Friday last, when the C.B.C. gave the first intimation it intended to defy the order of the B.B.G. We are raising the matter in the house at the first opportunity.
There are precedents to which I could refer, when previous Speakers have permitted a debate to be launched under similar circumstances. I should like to refer to an occasion in March, 1961, when the Minister of Labour made a statement in the house on a Thursday affecting the areas of double depreciation. On Friday the matter was raised in a motion by the Leader of the Opposition, and the Speaker permitted a debate notwithstanding the fact that it was announced by the Prime Minister that the estimates of the Department of Labour might be coming before the house within a week.
In this case we had a sudden emergency occasioned on Friday; there is no listing on the order paper or any intimation by the government than an opportunity will be given to debate this subject matter. For these reasons I suggest that the requirements of rule 26 are fully satisfied in so far as the question of urgency of debate is concerned.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say briefly just two things about the urgency of debate. The first is that the issue before us is the question of whether the board of broadcast governors has the right to compel the C.B.C. to carry the advertising that goes with the game-Mr. Speaker, do not shake your head -and that issue arose only a few days ago, so the opposition could not possibly have debated this issue on the last supply motion or on any other previous occasion.
The second point I wish to make, Mr. Speaker, arises out of the remarks made by the hon. member for Peace River, the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister. He draws attention to the fact that a number of questions have been asked, and that this process has been going on for a number of days. This illustrates the very point we are
[Mr. MacEachen.l

trying to make, namely the need for debate on this question. The answers we have received to those questions have made it very clear that it has not been possible for the high court of parliament, to which these two bodies are responsible, to discuss this matter. It is because parliament has had no chance to discuss it that we feel it is urgent we have an opportunity to debate this subject and discuss an issue which has arisen and which is in our view very important.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I should like to make a brief observation on two points which have been raised. The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond says there is no alternative opportunity for debate. This is only a small part of what is involved in the determination of the urgency of debate. Of course there will, at some stage, be an opportunity for debate, but this does not go to the question of urgency. What is urgent about this?
If this is the kind of public dispute that it is described as being, Mr. Speaker, then it might be going on for some time. Parliament does not settle that and remove the problem by the discussion of a motion of this kind. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam spoke of the need for this house to issue an order to the board of broadcast governors. This house has no authority to issue an order to the board of broadcast governors. It is parliament that has set up the board of broadcast governors and given it certain powers and functions. This house cannot interfere with any of the powers given to that statutory body for the discharge of these functions.
There is no urgency for discussion, therefore, of this matter at this time. There is no urgency that presents itself in that connection, because a debate would not settle anything. There is no immediate issue that presents a need for debate at this time. (Translation):

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should have liked to have such a great number of friends in the opposition to defend the 92,000 Quebec farmers who earn only $1,900 a year. Since those people will not even be able to listen to the radio broadcast of the Grey cup game, I believe that in the circumstances it is not in order to waste half an hour of the time of the house to discuss whether or not that game should be shown on television.
(Text):

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I have examined the motion that is before me, and I would preface my remarks in respect of it by saying it is recognized, and has been recognized over

many years, that this section 26 of our standing orders is a remedy to be used only under very extraordinary circumstances. Then the house agrees to set aside its routine business to discuss a certain matter which cannot wait.
I wish to thank hon. members for the various arguments they have addressed to me on this point. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre felt that the issue was a conflict, but I cannot read the motion in that way because it says the definite matter of urgent public importance is the need to provide parliament with full information. The motion then goes on to merely identify the nature of the information.
Well, one could go into the pros and cons of the conflict, but that is not the issue today. We have two bodies which are in discussion over a particular athletic event; and whether its telecast will be carried with advertising or without advertising or with other complications or lack of complications does not enter into the question at the moment.
This house could not give any directions nor could it get any information this afternoon to assist in the resolution of the problem, and I rather fear it would only lead to an expression of individual opinions as to whether one should do this or that. According to my view that is not the burden of the motion. The burden of the motion is the need to provide information. As to the urgency of debate, I have not heard anyone suggest that there has been a refusal to supply information.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Yes, there has.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: Whether information has been sought is one question; whether full information has been sought is another, and whether information has been sought in a proper manner is a third. It is my view that neither on the score of urgent importance nor on the score of urgency of debate does this motion meet the requirements of standing order No. 26. Therefore I cannot accept the motion for adjournment of the house on this occasion.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minisier of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. C-79, to amend the Estate Tax Act.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Chown in the chair.
Clauses 1 to 5 inclusive agreed to.
On clause 6-Lien for taxes.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I could have a word of explanation from the minister as to what they are doing here in this clause. I think the clause is probably a very good one, but I am still not too clear as to exactly what they are trying to do. I wondered if we might have a word of explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as the hon. member and the committee know, the Minister of National Revenue has a lien on real property in connection with any unpaid balance of estate tax. Sometimes it is very, very difficult, in connection with the lien, to ascertain what are the conditions of the title from the records. Therefore this is a remedial section in order to assist people in the transfer of property. I might very briefly read the statement which I have in front of me. It is not in technical language. To help remove this difficulty in establishing clear title, the amendment in paragraph (1) restricts the present provision so that a lien will apply only where it can be ascertained

from the records of the land registry office that a deceased person had an interest in the real property that is being transferred.
In other words, unless the record office shows definitely that the deceased person had an interest in the real estate, the lien does not apply. There are cases where, as hon. members know, the records do not show this clearly. If they do not, a purchaser can take title to a property without having the impact of a lien upon him.
One further question: what is the arrangement under this clause for releasing a lien claim where a province enters a contract with the dominion government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is covered by a subclause. To go one step further in the explanation I gave a moment ago, I indicated that sometimes it was difficult to get an accurate picture by searching the records. Various provinces have different systems of registration. This clause provides that where a province agrees not to permit the transfer of real property after the death of a deceased property owner until it is satisfied that the Minister of National Revenue has been paid, there is no necessity for a lien and no obligation on a purchaser. The three provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba have in practice already adopted this procedure. If this clause is approved and an argreement with a province is made, the registrar will not transfer title until he is satisfied the Minister National Revenue has been paid. Once that payment has been recorded, the purchaser knows that the property is free from estate tax.
I should like to congratulate the minister on behalf of the legal profession. This provision will go a long way toward meeting the difficulties which have arisen in this respect.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 7-

I wonder if the minister would explain the type of conversation which is likely to take place under the provisions of clause 7? Is this an indication that people who go to departmental representatives and speak frankly with them can be guided and assisted? I wonder if the minister would help us by giving the committee a little further explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I understand this clause, the right to get information only applies at the moment to a person who has entered an objection or an appeal. He must be on record before he can seek this information. Excise Tax Act

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-80 to amend the Excise Tax Act.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Chown in the chair.
On clause 1-Definitions.

I wish, Mr. Chairman, to say something generally about this bill. Bill No. C-80 is intended, I believe, to close a loophole with regard to insurance premiums tax which, I presume, is not in contradiction of our tax agreements with other countries, and to make certain other technical amendments to the act.
In respect of this act, the Minister of Finance stated in this house on November 9 last, and I quote from Hansard at page 1489 of that date:
When I first became Minister of National Revenue and started to inquire about the Excise Tax Act I was told by a very distinguished and a very senior civil servant: "Don't try to understand it; it does not make any sense at all."
And I have never tried to understand it since.
This is a remarkable admission from the Minister of Finance who now comes before
17G8

Excise Tax Act
this house and asks us to make a few technical amendments to the act through Bill C-80. I have reviewed these amendments and I can assure the house that they do nothing to make the act more sensible to me as a layman.
I would like to assert that this government has been derelict in its duty to the Canadian people with respect to the Excise Tax Act. The tax implications of this act are important to every Canadian citizen in that through it the government imposed taxes which amounted to $1,413 million in 1962. The Minister of Finance has admitted that it makes no sense and yet he comes before this house asking us to continue this law subject to the few minor changes proposed in Bill C-80.
Last week the Minister of Finance indicated that the Income Tax Act has become so complicated that he cannot understand it. When my hon. friend from Davenport suggested that it be immediately rewritten the minister flatly refused to have persons undertake this important task. I am not sure of the basis of this refusal but I presume it has something to do with the fact that we have sitting a royal commission on taxation.
I maintain that this same argument is not valid in the case of the Excise Tax Act. On July 5, 1955, a sales tax committee was appointed under the chairmanship of Mr. Ken Carter, who has now been appointed chairman of the royal commission on taxation, and he reported to the then minister of finance on January 12, 1956. The committee received 38 submissions and carefully considered them before reporting. Members of the commission also went to Australia and to Washington at public expense during the course of their deliberations.
The government has had five years to consider the conclusion of this committee and to come up with an excise tax act which does make sense. They have failed to carry out this task and I maintain that their failure to do so is a flagrant neglect of their duty to Canadian taxpayers.
Before I conclude I would like to point out that one of the chief deficiencies in the Excise Tax Act to which attention was drawn by the committee was the fact that there are more than 25 references to ministerial discretion in the present act. This can result in taxation without specific approval of the House of Commons and without the right of appeal to the courts. It can lead to unfairness in the application of this tax as between taxpayers. I call on the Minister of Finance to proceed forthwith in the revision of the Excise Tax Act without waiting for five years for the royal commission on taxation to report and to have this report considered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I made a mistake in extending the courtesy to the hon. gentleman of letting him speak after he was asleep.
He was up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He was not up. Nevertheless, what he said with respect to the Carter committee of 1955 was that it reported in 1956. Hence there was only one year between 1956 and 1957. You would not expect the lethargic government of that day to take any steps at all in that year. But during the intervening years steps have been taken. I have not the figure in front of me at the moment, but a number of the recommendations of the Carter committee have been implemented by the government of the day. No doubt there is opportunity for amending from time to time any statute. I am not questioning that fact. However, I say that the report of the Carter committee was considered carefully by the officers of the Department of Finance and where it was felt possible or practical under the circumstances existing from time to time the recommendations of the Carter committee have been implemented. We are now considering some recommendations, not of the Carter committee itself per se but some amendments which are essential for the efficient administration of the act.

I should like to impress upon the minister the suggestion that was inherent in the question which I asked of the Prime Minister on the orders of the day today. It refers in particular to a telegram which it is my understanding was addressed to the Prime Minister yesterday by the manager and general counsel of the All Canada Insurance Federation. In order to put the matter in full perspective I think I might read that telegram to the minister. It reads as follows:
Recognizing the potential problems which might arise in implementing paragraph 8 of the Excise Tax Act resolution All Canada Insurance Federation whose member companies write 90 per cent of the automobile casualty and fire premiums in Canada requested an interview with the Minister of Finance by letter dated August 15. On September 18 the minister replied intimating an interview would be arranged later that month. No interview has yet been granted. Bill C-80 as presented for first reading to the House of Commons does not resolve the problems which were anticipated and will result in difficulties for government and the insurance industry alike. All Canada Insurance Federation again requests an opportunity to submit its representations to the government and undertakes to co-operate in seeking a practical solution. Wtih all due respect All Canada Insurance Federation submits it is in the interest of the government as well as the public and the insurance industry that further consideration of Bill C-80 be deferred until our representations may be heard and considered.

The reply of the Prime Minister to my question was that ample opportunity had been afforded to the industry to make its representations. I think it is implicit from the telegram I have just read that, far from ample opportunity having been afforded, the government appears to have been evading any opportunity of speaking with the representatives of the industry. I would therefore submit to the minister that in all good conscience and in all good reason he should defer further action on clause 1 until he has had an opportunity of hearing the views of a very considerable portion of the Canadian insurance industry on this particular clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In that connection, I might say that this resolution, of course, was brought in last April. Representations were made, so I am told. I am not conversant with them personally. As to that date, I am told that representations were made by various parties to the minister of the day and to the officers of the department. I also have received representations in connection with it. These representations have all been given the most careful consideration and as a result of those representations and the consideration by the government the bill is brought forward in the form in which it is now before the committee.

I should like to ask the Minister of Finance this question. If some of the Carter committee recommendations have been implemented, does he still stand by his statement of last Friday, that this bill or this act-I refer to the Excise Tax Act-as such does not make sense? I should also like him to inform this committee at some time, perhaps now or before we get through third reading, just what recommendations of the Carter committee have been written into the Excise Tax Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend carries very much weight in the house if all he has to criticize is some facetious remark of mine at one time. I am sure it is a very good bill. That is the only question. Perhaps I should have said "illogical" instead of "did not make sense". There are many illogical sections in the bill, owing to the exemptions which have come in during the years. However, that is a matter which has developed over many years. I am sure any predecessor of mine in either government could say exactly the same thing.

I have listened with considerable interest to the remarks of the hon. member for Kingston and the reply of the minister in connection with what the hon. member for Kingston has had 27507-3-1124
Excise Tax Act
to say. I must say I was rather impressed with the statement made a few moments ago by the hon. member for Kingston, as indeed I have been impressed with a number of the observations and speeches he has made in this house. The hon. member for Kingston is obviously a man of considerable authority in matters having to do with taxation. We listen to what he says, recognizing that his are the words of someone who has authority in this field.
I do not believe the minister is warranted in the criticism he has made of the hon. member. In the first place, the hon. gentleman obviously could not have been asleep, as his remarks were so well put together that only a wide awake man could make them. Every one of the statements made on clause 1 of the bill was perfectly in order; they were just as much in order as they would have been if they had been made when Mr. Speaker was in the chair. The Minister of Finance need not be piqued by the observations of the hon. member. These observations were made because, as a tax expert and as professor in matters of taxation he is greatly concerned with the loose way in which this act is being formulated.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By your government.

It does not matter by whom. He is greatly concerned with the way in which this act is being formulated and the way in which it continues to be administered by the present administration.
The Minister of Finance may be an estimable gentleman, and we all recognize that fact. However, he happens to be the Minister of Finance and on his shoulders reposes a responsibility which he must discharge in order not to impose needlessly on the people of this country taxes which now are heavy and which should not be imposed, if by careful formulation of legislative enactments we can avoid this added burden. That is what the hon. member for Kingston had in mind.
He pointed out that the Carter committee made its report in 1956. That report was in the hands of the former administration for less than a year. It has been in the hands of the present administration for over five years. Faced with some 25 recommendations made by this committee, the minister has simply replied to the hon. member by saying that some of these recommendations have been adopted. In spite of a second question by the hon. member for Kingston, as to which of the recommendations have been adopted, we have not had any reply from the minister.
On a matter of taxation, something that involves the imposition of heavy pecuniary obligations on the Canadian people, surely

Excise Tax Act
this House of Commons is entitled to know what particular recommendations have been accepted by the goverment. Since 1957, there has been no reference in any budget speech to the Carter committee by the former minister of finance. Consequently, now that this matter has been raised, we should have from the minister a precise statement as to which of these various 25 recommendations have been implemented. If the minister will indicate which recommendations have been carried out I think we may draw the conclusion that possibly his own knowledge of the act is much greater than that which he, in in his own modesty the other day, suggested was the case. I am giving the minister an opportunity to show that he really does know a good deal about this act by telling us precisely which recommendations have been accepted by the government.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I am anticipating the reply that the minister will give to the hon. member for Kingston but in his initial remarks he referred in particular to the question whether or not the proposed amendment might be a violation of the Canada-United States reciprocal tax convention and the similar convention between Canada and the United Kingdom. I would refer the minister in particular to article 1 of the United States convention and articles 1 and 2 of the United Kingdom convention. The argument basically would be that, if this is a tax imposed upon premium income, then is this not a tax imposed upon profits arising outside of Canada in respect of a corporation which does not for the purpose of these profits have a permanent establishment in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I hesitate to give a legal opinion. I am advised by the officials that this is not in conflict in any way at all with our statutory obligations.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?
Are we not going to get from the minister some indication as to what his answers are to the question put by the hon. member for Kingston?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at this moment.

Mr. Chairman, as I read clause 1 it will represent a greater burden on consumers ini Canada. What were the circumstances and the pressures that prompted this particular amendment? Can the minister indicate to us what the additional revenue is expected to be from this additional tax imposed on Canadian users of insurance, and what were the reasons? Who were the people interested in having this additional burden

imposed on Canadians generally. I think it has been the custom, certainly in years past, and I am thinking of around the year 1900, never to let tax measures go by without having a pretty clear indication from the minister as to who is to benefit, who is going to have to pay and what the reasons are for the redistribution. Is this something that is going to be of great advantage to the treasury?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Which clause is the hon. member on?
Clause 1.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I assume the hon. member is discussing the clause in relation to insurance premiums. As was stated by the former minister of finance during the budget speech, the purpose of the proposal is to discourage the placing of insurance with non-resident agents, in many cases in the United States, I think. What was envisaged was the placing of Canadian holdings of insurance with nonresident agents outside of Canada and it is to discourage this sort of thing that we have this provision before us. From the point of view of the actual increase in revenue, it has to be admitted that while there is an increase involved the amount of increase in revenue from the implementation of this proposal will be small. I did not quite follow the hon. member in his reference to an added burden on Canadians but maybe I am ahead of myself.

I thank the parliamentary secretary for his assistance. I take it that what this really represents in the tax field is another element of protectionism. In other words, it is an additional wall by way of protection to the carrying on of such business in Canada against competition from outside. I am interested in the observations of the parliamentary secretary. It was my thinking that this would be more detrimental to British companies than to United States companies, but is the minister or the parliamentary secretary satisfied that this provision will not add to the cost of insurance in any material way? The parliamentary secretary says that there will be virtually no benefit to the treasury. I should like to know who will derive the benefit. Obviously we are now operating very much in the red in this country and it is hard to understand why we add taxes unless it is for the purpose of increasing the income of the treasury. If this is not so, who is going to benefit from this provision and will the effect be to bring about less competition in the insurance field than there now is?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Offhand I would say to the hon. member that I cannot see where anything in this provision will make the insurance field less competitive.

Mr. Chairman, there is one thing that I do not like about this bill. In the new section 6 under clause 1 it is provided that the superintendent or any officer of his department appointed by him may visit the office of any insurer, broker or agent and examine his books, etc. That means this is another instance of some kind of police state being brought about in Canada. An official can go into any office, take the man's books without his consent, look them over and take them away just as is done under the Income Tax Act. I believe we have too much of that already and we should take a good look at it. I do not think the officials were careful enough in drafting this bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

Has the parliamentary
secretary no comment to make on the observations of the hon. member for Hull?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I have no particular comment to make on his remarks.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What about the minister?

Do you not think this is going a little too far? An agent or an insurer has a contract to deal with insurance in Canada and generally he is sworn in every year when he takes out his licence. He has to report to the insurance department of the province in which he is carrying on business if he has dealt with companies not licensed to operate in Canada. The provinces have these regulations; so why should the superintendent of insurance have the right at any time to send officials into an office and take over everything they find there as is done in police states? I do not believe that should be done in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, only one word is added to this section. The principle was approved a year ago and there is only a very minor change. With regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Hull concerning the police authority of the superintendent of insurance, that is not a matter on which I would want to comment at the moment. Many officials have powers of inspection which parliament in its wisdom has decided they should be endowed with. The superintendent of insurance is an official who has been occupying that position for many years and I believe that generally speaking parliament and the country have confidence in the actions he takes.
If I remember correctly, when the Conservatives were on this side of the house they were opposed to this but now they are on the other side they favour it and have increased the power.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. C-81, to amend the Customs Tariff.

Mr. Speaker, the bill before us to amend the Customs Tariff is of course an annual bill, because usually after the presentation of a budget several financial statutes of the country require amendment. This is one of them. The particular bill which is before us would not appear to be very important this year. It brings back, six months after the presentation of the budget, the exact amendments of the former minister of finance with respect to the Customs Tariff. The new minister does not propose any amendment, despite the serious situation that has developed between April and now, and indeed which developed between April and June 24, after the election. Despite this, no further ideas are presented in this bill. I say that therefore this bill, on the face of it, may not appear too important to hon. members. But I say we must look beyond the bill, because something very important has occurred since the budget was presented on April 20.
The executive, by order in council after the election, took steps with respect to the statute we are now considering, the Customs Tariff, of very great consequence not only to parliament, having regard to parliament's rights, but to the Canadian people as a whole, because the Prime Minister, in a press release after the austerity measures were announced to the Canadian people, made it known that under the statute which is now before us the executive proposed to tax the Canadian people on a full year basis to the extent of $200 million; and there is no suggestion yet on the part of this administration that they want ratification and approval by parliament of that imposition of taxation.
Shameful, too.

Two hundred million dollars were involved by this executive act of June 24 by order in council. Orders in council were condemned year in and year out by some of the present ministry when they sat in opposition. We have always thought it fundamental that the House of Commons had to be taken into consideration when there was a question of the imposition of taxation.
Revolutions have been fought over that.

We have been here eight weeks. Many months went by during this so-called cooling off period after the election before the calling of parliament on September 27. But there has been no suggestion

whatever that in connection with this imposition of taxes to the extent of $200 million parliament is going to be asked this session to approve the action taken, or indeed that we are to be given any opportunity even to discuss it. I said that the schedule attached to this bill in this particular year does not appear impressive. The former minister of finance, when he introduced the resolutions in April, indicated that each of the tariff changes proposed was to reduce tariffs; there were no increases involved in the schedule attached to this bill. That may have been valid in April. But, ignoring parliament, in the meantime by executive action through order in council we have substantial increases in tariffs. Surely the house is concerned with this question.
I want to be brief, Mr. Speaker, but I do not think any hon. member of this house could read the two basic statutes upon which the June 24 order in council was based without coming to the conclusion that the executive, the cabinet, stretched to the limit and beyond the limit any powers parliament might have had in contemplation when the relevant sections were made the law of the land. I am not going into detail at this time with respect to them, but I wish to say to the house that, first of all, the cabinet took upon themselves the right to cancel or change every concession that had been made over the years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether I could refer Your Honour to the fact that this particular aspect of the debate which is engaging the attention of the hon. member has been the subject of discussion and decided upon in connection with an amendment which was moved by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacEachen) on October 5 with regard to this issue.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. gentleman read the motion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. The motion was:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that the failure of Your Excellency's advisers to place before this house at the earliest opportunity a measure to approve the collection of taxes which have been imposed by order in council, as part of the austerity program, denies to this house the exclusive constitutional right to approve the imposition of additional taxation which is the foundation of our system of responsible government.
It does seem that this particular aspect of the issue is the one which is engaging the attention of the hon. member.

May I speak to the point of order? This subject is not before the House of Commons today through the initiative of 27507-3-113
Customs Tariff
the opposition. It is before us by reason of an amending bill initiated by the government to the Customs Tariff Act. In the schedule attached to the bill Your Honour will find items which, I say, may have been valid in April, and realistic in so far as they apply to tariff rates applicable to the items under discussion; but today I say this house cannot pass either the bill or the schedule attached to it without recognizing the fact that in the meantime some of these items have been subjected to a surcharge imposed by order in council on June 24.
I submit that the normal rule preventing us from discussing the same subject twice in the same session does not apply when we have a bill designed to amend a statute, a bill which has been introduced by the government and one which is in its present form unrealistic because the rates in the schedule are now subject to certain surcharges imposed subsequent to the budget last April.

I should like to say a word about the point of order and about what was said by the parliamentary secretary. The hon. gentleman referred to a motion which had been moved expressing a lack of confidence in the government because it had imposed surcharges in certain circumstances. That question was dealt with, and I agree that as a subject for an expression of want of confidence in the government the house has made a decision-a decision which cannot be further discussed at this time. But what my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson) is presenting to the house are arguments with respect to the bill which is before us, and it is with respect to this bill that he is referring to certain things which were done by the government. He is not directing his argument to whether or not the government deserves confidence because of those things. He is talking about the government's actions in relation to this particular bill.
In addition, we had a categorical undertaking which was given by the minister to my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River in committee on November 12, and I draw Your Honour's attention to page 1521 of Hansard where the minister is reported as saying, when my hon. friend sought to discuss the surcharges at that time:
I anticipated that the hon. member would raise this point, and I am glad to see that he is not in a panic in any way. I would suggest that when we get into the bill I would then be better prepared to answer these questions, which he knows are rather difficult to answer at this stage of the debate and on this day.
That was a day when there was a statutory holiday and when there were none of the

Customs Tariff
officials present. In order to make clear that there was no misunderstanding, I got up and said:
I think the position taken by the minister, in all the circumstances, is a most reasonable one, and I take it that if we forgo any lengthy discussion today we shall not be faced with any entanglement of points of order and things of that sort at a later stage.
The minister nodded his head in approval at that point.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Are we still speaking on the point of order in which it is suggested that this is something new, without repetition? I think, in considering this point of order, it must be borne in mind that we cannot repeat a discussion under any guise whatsoever; we cannot bring in some principle under a new guise; we definitely have a rule against repetition and, certainly, debate on one matter cannot resurrect debate which existed on the same matter in other circumstances.
I do not think, though, that the hon. member is precluded from adverting to the surcharges. However, I think he would be precluded from discussing at length the legality or illegality of those charges, or matters related to the surcharges themselves. That is not an issue here. The hon. member's point is that this bill purports to deal with certain items in the Customs Tariff although those particular items have been changed since the month of April. As long as the hon. member does not revive argument as to the legality of the surcharges, because he cannot do that, I think it is all right for him to go ahead. But I put it to hon. members that we cannot repeat the debate which took place on a supply motion a short time ago, and the Chair will be very strict in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to say, in this connection, that the motion to which the hon. member for Peace River drew our attention was a motion made at the time of the debate on the address. I should like to point out to Your Honour that since then this house decided that whatever might be said as to the legality or illegality of the surcharges they should not be removed at this time. That represents another decision of the house made on the supply motion the other night. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) put forward a motion dealing with that, among other things. So whether the charges are legal, or whether they apply or not, the house has decided that they are not to be removed at this time.
It is true I told the hon. member the other day in reply to a question that I would be glad to deal with the matter. The only way I can do that is in committee, where I could tell

him to which, if any, of these items, the surcharges apply. I am prepared to do that when we get into committee, without raising points of order.

I listened with interest to what Your Honour had to say. With respect, I think there is some confusion as to the procedural point involved. The question, which was before the house on another occasion, and which is now held up as an obstacle to proceeding along the lines which my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River was pursuing was an amendment moved by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacEachen) having to do with what was alleged to be a violation of constitutional practice. The legality of the surcharges was another point altogether which had nothing to do with the amendment. It is true that on that amendment I did discuss the legality of the surcharges as well as the substance of the amendment, contending that the failure of the government to take parliament into its confidence was a violation of constitutional practice. But the legality of the surcharges is a matter which has not yet been determined in this house pursuant to any amendment.
There is at the present time a motion before the house asking for the production of papers which touches the legality of the surcharges. That, too, is a motion involving a different matter from the subject matter which led to the remarks made by my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River.

speakeroldname: Mr. Malcolm Maclnnis (Cape Breton South) moved:
subsubtopic: DEVELOPMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the concrete implementation of a long range, positive and comprehensive program of economic development for the Atlantic provinces of Canada, and to provide, in particular, for the following short range and long-term measures:
(1)	To assure that existing employment in the basic iron, coal and steel industry be fully protected until alternative employment opportunities can be developed in the region;
(2)	To launch a major program of public capital construction in co-operation with the provincial governments; and,
(3)	To establish a department of Atlantic development, responsible for the overall co-ordination of efforts by all federal departments and agencies in the formulation of positive, long range and comprehensive measures designed to promote the economic rehabilitation of the Atlantic region, and for the administering of a large scale development fund for financing the creation of essential industrial capital.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention this evening to go into this particular resolution in any great detail. As a result of the opportunity which was mine to participate in the throne speech debate I have already outlined some of the history and the present factors associated with the economic problems of the Atlantic provinces.
The purpose of this particular resolution is to provide for the planned, co-ordinated and directed long range economic development of that part of Canada which has not shared in the general economic development we have experienced in Canada, in general, from the days of confederation. In this connection, the government have indicated their intention to establish an Atlantic development board. I am sure that all of the people in this part of Canada welcome this announcement by the government, at least in so far as it represents an indication on the part of the government that they are aware of the situation in the Atlantic provinces. But, Mr. Speaker, as I have already suggested during the throne speech debate, if it is the intention of the government simply to set up another body to conduct research and various programs of study and to make suggestions, then I suggest to you that this procedure is going to take altogether too much time and that it is not really going to get at the root of the matter. Therefore, in this resolution I am suggesting that, while most certainly we desire a program of economic development, such a program should be under the direction and within the scope of the responsibility of a
1778	HOUSE OF
Proposed Maritime Industrial Development particular minister of the crown. The Atlantic development board could then, I suggest, very efficiently, logically and acceptably work with this minister as they attempt to take action to implement the program of economic development in co-operation with the provincial governments of these four provinces.
There are some people who suggest that the Atlantic provinces of Canada are not the only sections of the country which experience particularly depressing economic conditions. This of course is a fact. However, we can say in general that wherever we find depressed pockets in other parts of Canada, it is generally within the midst of industries which are operating successfully to some extent. I suggest to the members of the house that only in the Atlantic provinces do we have a unique situation where the entire region is so greatly depressed that when industries such as coal and steel are declining there is no opportunity for the people who have been employed in those industries over the years to seek alternative employment in the same area. This problem is, of course, expanded in a situation such as that which we have in Canada today. When these people are forced to leave the Atlantic provinces, in view of the unemployment situation in the country at large, it is extremely difficult for them to find alternative employment even in other parts of the country.
We in the Atlantic provinces of Canada are not pessimists. We believe that our part of Canada can come into its own. Many of our people see a tremendous economic future for the Atlantic area. For a long time the Atlantic provinces have been awaiting the hand of development. We have much in the way of untapped and underdeveloped resources. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the industrial concerns of the country that, in view of the new trading patterns being established around the world, the Atlantic provinces are once again, as they were prior to confederation, going to be in the forefront of future economic developments in Canada.
There are some who suggest that we in this part of Canada should be able to lift ourselves by our own bootstraps. However, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to you that we have done everything it is possible for us to do by ourselves. Various research projects have been conducted very successfully and very informatively by the Atlantic provinces economic council. We have self-help economic development organizations such as Industrial Estates Ltd. in Nova Scotia. However, I suggest to you that, in view of all these efforts


of the people of the Atlantic area to lift themselves up by their own bootstraps, it has now finally and irrevocably been established that federal government assistance is required.
We are not asking for very much. We are asking simply for equality of opportunity for our people in that part of the nation. We are asking equal wages for equal work. For example, we are asking equal wages for the teachers in the Atlantic provinces as compared with those of teachers in the wealthier parts of Canada. We desire equality in wages for the marine workers, the steel workers and so on. In brief, we are asking that the people in the Atlantic provinces be permitted to share in the benefits of confederation. We are asking that we be permitted to develop economically, so that we can provide a decent standard of living for our people and so that we can provide them with equal municipal services with an equal burden of taxation.
In suggesting that there is a tremendous economic future for the Atlantic provinces we are saying that, with the aid of the federal government, new industries can be attracted into that area and that those new industries can be developed. In line with the research of the Atlantic provinces economic council and in line with the program of the New Democratic party-and we have been saying this now since our founding-I suggest to you that, in developing the economy of the Atlantic provinces, it is essential that we establish certain cornerstone industries which will allow us to develop a stable economy and which in turn will attract other minor and secondary manufacturing establishments. Keeping in mind this principle of key cornerstone industries-and this is absolutely essential to any future economic development- I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, as is outlined in this particular resolution, that we cannot be successful unless we protect the existing basic industries in the area. I am from a particular part of Nova Scotia. There are other members here from other parts of the Atlantic provinces who can expand on some of the other industries. However, I am here referring particularly to the basic industries of coal and steel. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that we cannot neglect these most important potential cornerstone industries in any long range economic program.
We were very happy to see the federal government announce, in April of this year, a special subsidy on coal of 30 cents per ton because, from the point of view of competitive advantage, this provided to our coal industry an opportunity to compete with imported foreign oil. We would suggest that the federal government should keep this special subsidy under review and expand it

as necessary so as to ensure that the tremendous potential existing tor coal in the thermal power field, certainly within the Atlantic provinces, will be exploited in order that our generation of thermal power will be based on coal.
There are many people in Canada who suggest that, apart from new potential uses for coal, some of the traditional markets may well be restored to the coal industry. I should like to paraphrase here a statement that was made recently at the Canadian coal conference. Many economists see coal regaining some of the industrial markets it has been losing to gas and oil simply because both gas and oil are becoming scarcer in North America. The unit price is rising and in future it can go nowhere but up.
So, Mr. Speaker, we suggest first that the coal industry in Canada, certainly in the eastern part of Canada, is not dead. There is a tremendous future for coal. Coal is one of our important basic resources and it has a future even within the framework of the traditional markets and traditional uses for coal. But I would suggest to you that what is even more important and even more encouraging to us in the Atlantic provinces is the tremendous possibilities that are held out for coal in the thermal power field. We are told, for example, that by 1980, in the not too distant future, the market for coal for use by Ontario hydro alone will be in the neighbourhood of 26 million tons.
An experiment is at present being conducted in Dartmouth, Nova Scotia, under the auspices of the national research council to investigate the competitive price situation of coal used in the generation of thermal power to supply domestic home heating as opposed to other forms of electricity. We are going to be very interested in the results of this study because, on the basis of present and existing information, limited as it is, there is a very strong indication that there is a tremendous opportunity for coal in the industrial, commercial and domestic home heating fields.
There are other aspects I certainly do not have time to go into in the few minutes allotted to -me today. There are many other related factors that could very well provide the necessary impetus for the Atlantic provinces if we receive the necessary backing from the federal government in the field of thermal power development. For example, the Du Pont Company of Canada is now studying the possibility of establishing a heavy water plant somewhere in Canada. We are informed that, apart from other requirements for such an industry, which we know are being looked into in the province of Nova Scotia at the present time, such as 50,000
gallons of water per minute, there is a tremendous possibility that the by-product steam from a thermal generating plant could be used to supply the cheap power needed for such a heavy water plant. This is one of the possible related economic developments that could come about in the Atlantic provinces, if we take the necessary initiative in the whole field of thermal power.
Finally, with respect to coal, Mr. Speaker,
I should like to read into the record a statement by Mr. Berkovitz of the research council of Alberta when he was speaking about coal at the recent Canadian coal conference. He said:
In a world that has become conscious of the need to wisely use its natural endowments, it is simply no longer considered permissible to neglect a resource completely, merely because one of its major traditional uses has become obsolete.
In short, Mr. Speaker, as far as the coal industry is concerned we in the Atlantic provinces are very optimistic. There is a great future for coal if the federal government provides the proper type of assistance.
The second basic industry to which I refer in this resolution is the steel industry. I am not going to say very much about this industry, except to call attention to my earlier reference to the new trading patterns that are developing around the world. It seems to many of us in the Atlantic provinces that the steel industry of Nova Scotia is in a particularly ideal position in relation to the new expanding export market that is going to be ours in Canada.
We are all aware, of course, of the assistance that has been provided this industry under the terms of the Export Credits Insurance Act, and other possible arrangements are being negotiated at the present time. But we are very concerned about the steel industry in this part of Canada. There has been some suggestion that certain parts of the industry would be relocated in other areas of Canada. Once again, Mr. Speaker, within the framework of the necessary federal assistance that must be given we suggest, as envisaged in this resolution, that it would be a worth-while endeavour for the federal government to call a conference at which representatives of the provinces of Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia and the major steel companies in Canada would be present to discuss the entire steel industry in Canada. I bring this forward for this reason. If six individual nations in the old iron and steel community of Europe could sit down to discuss and plan the future economic development of their coal and steel industries, surely it is not too much to expect that within the boundaries of this single nation of Canada we can sit down and discuss the development
