Proposed Maritime Industrial Development of the steel industry to the benefit of all parts of Canada, keeping in mind the particular economic problems of the Atlantic provinces.
The second factor involved in the resolution is that we must have a long range program. It simply is no longer acceptable to go from year to year, from mine closure to mine closure, from lay-off to lay-off, from one industry shut-down to another industry shutdown, on a lackadaisical, haphazard basis with no over-all policy. I suggest in this resolution that the Atlantic development board proposed by the federal government can be a form of economic salvation for the Atlantic provinces if it is placed under the control of a minister of the crown and if those concerned will sit down and develop a long range program that will project into the future.
In this connection I suggest that what we need in this frame of reference is an economic development fund of $100 million to be administered by the minister in charge of this program, working with an Atlantic development board. If the government will take this type of initiative I am quite convinced that a sound, economic base can be developed in the Atlantic provinces, that a decent standard of living can be developed for our citizens, that underemployment can be wiped out, that unemployment can be brought down to what we would hope would be a national average, in the neighbourhood of 1 per cent, representing frictional unemployment, and so on. In this way the Atlantic provinces will be enabled to share in the general benefits that have accrued to the rest of the nation as a result of confederation.

First of all, Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate my hon. friend from Cape Breton South for providing this opportunity to talk generally about the economic development of the Atlantic provinces. The opening words of the resolution ring a familiar bell because these words, "a planned and comprehensive program of economic development for the Atlantic provinces", were used in the preliminary report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. I think it is essential to insist upon a planned and comprehensive approach to our problem, in contrast with sporadic reaction to sudden difficulties, in contrast with ad hoc expedients and the introduction of a sudden policy to quell a sudden clamour in one or several parts of the Atlantic provinces.
I think it is essential also to emphasize the importance of long range policies. The Atlantic provinces economic council, for example, has attempted to set a target for job creation in the Atlantic provinces. I feel it is necessary to set a long range target over the next ten


years, say, and our objective ought to be the creation of 200,000 new jobs. All this would do, Mr. Speaker, would be to reduce the level of unemployment in our area to tolerable national levels and remove underemployment; so really it is a modest, necessary and realistic target.
The words of the resolution proposed by my hon. friend have been used in other motions introduced in this house over the years by members from all sides of the house, depending on their location in the house at the particular time. I believe it is a good thing to bring forward the general problems of the Atlantic provinces. However, I should like to make two points in this connection. In the Atlantic provinces as a whole there are certain areas that are doing relatively well. I participated in a program in Halifax not so long ago with one of the hon. members for Halifax, in which one of the prominent citizens of that city told us that conditions were good there. Certainly, I would be the last person to ask that they be bad in order to justify any particular argument I was making at the time.
I believe this underlines the necessity of knowing that even in an area like the Atlantic provinces there are good areas but also that there are areas that are suffering from persistent, chronic unemployment, and that this prevails regardless of the general prosperity of the country. Within the Atlantic provinces themselves, there is necessity for pinpointing a program of development to deal with particularly hard hit areas. I would go further and say that in talking about the general problem of regional or area development, we ought to bear in mind that there are other communities in Canada as well, in addition to the Atlantic provinces, that have been hard it. What we really need is a national policy that would apply to areas of chronic unemployment, regardless of their location in the Atlantic provinces or in other parts of Canada. A truly national policy would receive, I believe, general support from the people of Canada as a whole and would certainly receive general support from this parliament.
I am interested in the terms of the resolution, and just before discussing the terms in detail I should like to comment briefly on the proposed Atlantic development board, a subject which will come before the house later during the discussion of another resolution. All I want to say is that the creation of this board will not, of necessity ensure that the kind of economic development proposed by my hon. friend will be carried out.

The first proposal in this resolution is that measures be taken to assure that existing employment in the basic iron, coal and steel industries be fully protected until alternative employment opportunities can be developed in the region. I note the words, that employment in coal and steel be protected until alternative employment can be provided elsewhere. This may be the policy of the New Democratic party, but it is certainly not Liberal. It is a defeatist conclusion to accept the gradual decline of the coal and steel industries and the necessity of replacing those lost opportunities by the creation of alternative jobs in other industries. I believe that the coal industry, for example, has declined to the minimum tolerable level at the present time. It has been the hardest hit industry in Canada. Since 1955 it has lost about one fifth its work force, and since this government came into office it has lost about a million and a half tons of its production. It has been a hard hit industry and has brought dislocation to several important counties in Nova Scotia including Cape Breton, Pictou, Cumberland and Inverness. A further decline in the coal industry is certainly not tolerable.
I do believe, along with my hon. friend for Cape Breton South, it will be possible in the future to maintain, if not to expand, coal production in the Nova Scotia fields. The notion of replacing declining job opportunities by new industries is deficient on another ground; it fails to take into account the needs of communities like Springhill, which has lost most of its coal mines. It does not take into account the needs of communities like Inverness, which has lost every coal mine it had and where today there is no industry. This is a town in which there were 700 men employed not too many years ago in the production of coal. Surely-and this is something about which I feel very strongly-this country cannot really be satisfied to tolerate languishing communities like Springhill and Inverness where there are no jobs at all or where there are very few jobs. What happens in such communities is clear. Municipal services are weakened. Community spirit is dying. Educational institutions are losing their strength and there is a general atmosphere of despair.
In the United Kingdom it was possible to breathe new life into the hard pressed coal areas, and one of the first things President Kennedy did, after his accession to office in the United States, was to establish an area re-development agency which had as its first task to try to do something about the hard pressed coal communities in Pennsylvania.

We shall make a great mistake in this country if we fail to realize the absolute necessity of doing something not only to maintain current employment but to put new life and vitality into communities that have lost everything because of changed technology, changed consumer tastes and progress in general. I shall not pursue the coal question further because surely at an early date it will be possible for hon. members from Nova Scotia to debate the coal industry fully on the estimates for the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. I may add it is surprising that we have not had a statement on coal policy from the government since the session opened. In fact none was made during the last session. It is long overdue and we hope to debate that policy at the earliest possible opportunity.
With reference to the iron and steel industry in Nova Scotia it seems to me the goal here certainly ought not to be stabilization. It ought to be expansion. The greatest prospect for industrial development in the area of Cape Breton county is through the expansion of the steel industry, and it ought to be regarded as the strongest cornerstone of any program in that area. That industry has several thousand employees and it ought to be encouraged, with the right form of government assistance, to diversify its operations and expand its work force. That should be one of the main objectives of a program of development in the Atlantic provinces, and in Nova Scotia in particular.
The second part of this motion asks the government "to launch a major program of public capital construction in co-operation with the provincial governments." This brings to mind the well recognized role of capital expenditures in the public sector of the economy. There is no necessity to argue with anybody in the house on the creative role in economic development that can be played by carefully selected public projects, projects that will ultimately put more into the economy than will be taken out of it.
The Canso causeway was a project that had been urged for many decades upon the federal authorities. It was ultimately undertaken at an expenditure of $15 million, and some people said it was really in response to provincial political pressure. That may have been so, but it was something more than that. It was a creative public project that improved the transportation system between Nova Scotia and Cape Breton and also led to large scale private investment in the causeway area owing to the creation of an ice-free natural harbour.
It may never be possible to estimate fully the economic impact of such public projects,

Proposed Maritime Industrial Development but certainly we ought to move on the side of daring rather than on that of caution, because what happened in the Canso area demonstrated that daring in this public sector of construction has led to development and will lead to greater development, and the public treasury will receive more out of that than it put into it in the form of the initial grant.
Why has action not been taken by the government to establish a capital fund for development? The proposal was made in the royal commission on economic prospects that a capital projects commission be established to administer, in co-operation with the provinces, essential public projects in the Atlantic provinces. My hon. friends on the other side of the house in their momentous and highly successful conclave in Moncton, prior to the 1957 election, listed the establishment of a capital projects commission as one of their main objectives. It was regarded as one of the great points of what was then believed to be "the Atlantic charter." Some five and a half years have gone by and, even though in the last parliament they had the greatest number of supporters any government ever had, no action was taken on the creation of the capital projects commission. Every party in the house supports that proposal. We know it is essential; but now we are getting a development board, a board without money. It is a board which will have no capital at its disposal, such as is called for by this motion.
What is even more surprising than the government's inaction on the capital development fund is the inexplicable action in its austerity program in reducing capital construction in the Atlantic provinces. Surely one of the things we have learned from development programs in other countries is that where there is high, chronic unemployment, persisting over a period of time, capital expenditure must be undertaken. Here was an opportunity for the government to give recognition to that policy and say "If general reduction in capital spending is required, it will not be undertaken in areas of chronic unemployment where capital spending is needed more than in any other part of Canada."
We ought to move quickly to set up a capital fund that would be available to finance sound public projects and possibly participate in the financing of sound private projects that will lead to the development of greater opportunities in these provinces.
The third item dealt with in the motion is the setting up of a separate ministry, a separate department of government, to be responsible for the administration of an over-all program of development in the Atlantic


provinces. That proposal has been made by others, including the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon) and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), and the idea has been suggested, if not fully approved, by the leader of the Liberal party.

Mr. Speaker, I learned long since that it does not pay to get involved in discussions of points of order. If hon. gentlemen are interested in points of order, it is easier to discuss the matter and get on with the merits rather than to raise points of order. But I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the hon. gentleman that there are only two items subject to surcharge. I promised that when in committee I would refer to any items that were surcharged. There are only two items subject to surcharge, namely aircraft and aircraft engines. The purport of this bill is to remove the tariff charge which otherwise would be imposed on those two items. They are the only two items which are affected by the surcharge. If the hon. gentleman wishes to discuss the constitutional validity, something which has been determined twice by this House of Commons, I am not going to intervene since I know that the more time he spends on it, the more time he wastes. I say that subject to Your Honour's ruling.
However, I would suggest those are the only matters to which he can possibly make reference, and those are the two items which are covered by the surcharge, namely aircraft and aircraft engines. If this bill does not pass, then the tariff item which has been suspended for some years and which this bill proposes to suspend for another year will come into effect. The situation with respect to aircraft and aircraft engines will then be that they not only will be subject to the surcharge but also to a tariff of 15 per cent. They are the only items in the bill, which

Customs Tariff
after all is a relatively minor one with the smallest number of changes in my recollection.

I should like to say a word on the point of order since Your Honour has raised it, and it is this. What we are discussing on the second reading of the bill is whether or not the bill should be given second reading. That is the question before the house and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River in his line of argument is seeking to show, not just that one or two of the items in the schedule to the bill are affected by surcharges, which is a relatively minor point on which I agree with the Minister of Finance, but whether this parliament should be asked to give second reading to what the minister himself called a relatively minor bill, which makes a few small changes in the Customs Tariff that were forecast last April, while at the same time utterly ignoring the vast changes that have been made in the tariff by order in council and never brought before this house.
The fact that the house did not see fit to withdraw its confidence from the government because it had not brought these matters forward does not mean that it is not a good argument, I submit to Your Honour, to say that we should not proceed with the second reading of this bill until we have all the tariff changes before us.
In other words, the house should not be asked to deal with a few little raindrops when there is a whole bucket of water that we are not allowed to touch, if I may make a rather crude analogy. What the hon. member is saying, and surely this is a proper subject for debate on second reading, is that the government should not have brought in this little bill at all but should have brought in a big bill incorporating all of the changes that have been made in the Customs Tariff since the budget last April. That is what my hon. friend is arguing and it seems to me that is a perfectly proper line of argument with respect to whether or not we should give second reading to the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not going to deal with this point of order at any length, Mr. Speaker, but I should like to say on this matter that we had a motion with respect to the surcharges at the beginning of the session and you will remember that there was a vote of confidence. Then on the first motion to go into supply my hon. friend's leader and hon. gentlemen opposite all voted for the abolition of these surcharges; but the House of Commons in its wisdom decided that the surcharges should not be abolished at this time. Therefore, whatever the philosophical argument may be, I suggest that the house has 
decided on this matter. It has decided that it would be improper to remove the surcharges at this time and therefore the matter is not now subject to discussion at this stage on the second reading of this particular bill.

I would agree with the Minister of Finance if we were arguing that the surcharges should be removed. I would say that matter was settled by the house last week and it would be quite wrong to argue it. But the hon. member is not arguing that they should be removed. He is arguing that instead of this little bill, and the minister calls it a little bill, we should have a big bill so that parliament would validate all the Customs Tariff changes. We are not asking to have them removed. We accept the decision of the house made by hon. gentlemen opposite sdded by the Social Credit party that these surcharges should be retained. We accept that position. What we are saying is that this bill is not good enough by itself. We should have the whole gamut of these changes before us.

Mr. Speaker, for the moment I will deal only with the point of order as related to my own remarks. Under clause 1 of this bill, which we can deal with again, of course, in committee, we are dealing with the rates of duty set opposite each commodity item in the schedule. I am saying that these rates of duty have been materially affected by virtue of the cabinet action last June when by order in council certain surcharges were imposed. I want to say in addition that when we are amending the Customs Tariff I as a member of parliament am concerned about the basic act.
The government decided that they could do these certain things. They decided they could impose surcharges on $3 billion of imports at rates of 5, 10 or 15 per cent by executive action. They also decided last June that parliament should not be consulted about the matter and that it was none of parliament's business, even though in the revised budget estimates $200 million of taxation is involved.
With respect to the question of legality, I want to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance to the Financial Administration Act, section 22, which refers to opportunities to remit taxes. Parliament, under its authority with respect to taxation, decided some time ago that remission of taxes over a certain amount should be brought to the attention of all members of parliament and the way that is done is to draw attention to it in the public accounts.
We have a funny position imposed upon us by the executive, who say that they can do this in this way. The cabinet say that they can

remit taxes from the general tariff rate and to do this they rely on section 22 of the Financial Administration Act. It is provided in subsection 8 of section 22 of the Financial Administration Act that any remission of tax or duty that is given must be reported to parliament if the remission is in excess of $1,000. Under this fanciful order in council of June 24, when all remissions were to be scaled down from a general tariff rate-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member again and I accept responsibility for interrupting him before, but it seems to me we have had several opportunities to discuss the matters he is now bringing to the attention of the house in the past and it is quite conceivable in my mind that opportunities will arise again in the future. In all fairness, I find it very difficult to honour the rule of relevancy in my own mind, based on what the hon. member is discussing at the present time. I am thinking primarily of other members who probably wish to speak on second reading and how unfair it would be if I had to interrupt them in the same way.
I am loath to make a ruling because I know the hon. member is an experienced member of this house and I just ask for his co-operation with the Chair on the point of relevancy in respect of second reading.

I appreciate your predicament; but with respect I would suggest to you, in view of the fact you come from western Canada where air transportation on the cheapest possible basis is important, that you look at the schedule to this bill and appreciate the fact that the surcharge relates to items 440m and 440n. The point I am making is this, Mr. Speaker, that parliament passed the Financial Administration Act in which it is stated that under exceptional circumstances it would be possible for the cabinet to remit a tax or a duty and, for the protection of the members of this house, if there was a remission of consequence-one which involved something over $1,000-it would be reported to all of us in this assembly by an item in the public accounts.
I should like to ask the Minister of Finance, who was formerly the minister of national revenue, having regard to the item for remission in that order in council of June 24, is account being kept of the value of any remission of duty under the general tariff of $1,000 or more? I am informed that if one goes through the customs entry system he fills out a B-l entry form and there is no reference whatever to a remission from the unrealistic general tariff rate. Having regard to the order in council, I want to know whether the minister can assure this house
Customs Tariff
that in every instance if the value of the discount under the order in council is beyond $1,000, it will be reported to parliament in the public accounts. I hope the minister will also inform this house, during the debate on second reading of this bill, concerning the progress in tariff board considerations and what his predecessor said was the streamlining intended in respect to the Customs Tariff as a whole. I hope he will later refer to that.
I do not believe there is any member in this house, lawyer or layman, who reads the Financial Administration Act along with the order in council of June 24, who will say that tariff surcharges were justified, having regard to subsection 8 of section 22 which says that each remission of $1,000 or more granted under this section shall be reported to the House of Commons in the public accounts. All we have to do in that respect is to read the order in council of June 24. I challenge the minister to tell me that every customs entry point across this country has been keeping a record of all advantages given under the wording of the June 24 order in council that has a value beyond $1,000.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the discussions that have taken place on one or two points of order, I will make my remarks at this point brief. If I may say so, I was a little disturbed when the suggestion was being made from the Chair that because there had been previous discussions of the legality or otherwise of the surcharge order, we could not discuss that order again. I appreciate the refinement that I think you, sir, have now made in that respect. You have suggested that it might be possible to discuss that order on some other occasion but you prefer that the discussion do not take place now because you believe it is not particularly relevant to second reading of this bill.
I am doing what is sometimes done from the Chair: I am entering a caveat; I am staking out a right sometime later in this session, if it is not done while this bill is before us, to have a discussion on the legality of the surcharge order. In making that caveat and staking out that claim, I think I should point out that I differ from the Minister of Finance when he says that this matter has been decided. There have been the two votes in this house to which the Minister of Finance referred; one had to do with what the member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. MacEachen) called the constitutional position of the House of Commons in relation to the executive. The other had to do with whether or not the surcharges should be discontinued

Customs Tariff
forthwith. There have been votes on these two points expressing the opinion of the house, but there has been no vote on the question of whether or not the surcharge order is legally valid. I suggest that some time during this session, perhaps on the estimates of the Department of National Revenue or those of the privy council, we might have a discussion of this question if it is not settled in some other way. We are getting pretty close to it in the debate we are having on the motion for the tabling of the opinion of the law officer of the crown on the point.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, I for one appreciate the refinement you have made in the ruling in asking us to confine our discussion to this bill, reserving our right to discuss this matter on a later occasion. In that vein, I simply wish to say now that I think the government has a good deal of gall to come before parliament at this time with a bill to amend the Customs Tariff Act, and to put in it so little. This, of course, is a bill implementing what was proposed in the budget resolutions of last April, in the last session of another parliament. But in the meantime, these other changes have been made in the customs tariff situation. I think it is the height of gall for the government to come now with the same bill that was prepared last April, just as if there had been no other changes in the meantime. The fact that these two changes to impinge one upon the other is highlighted by the fact that there are at least two items-perhaps only two-that are in the bill and also in one of the schedules to the surcharge on imports orders. Surely that has led the Minister of Finance and the departments administering this into quite a kettle of fish.
What is the situation with respect to these items? The tariff on them said one thing prior to last April. Then in April changes were proposed and in June surcharges were imposed on them. Which is the rate of taxation? Is it the rate prior to last April or the rate as proposed by this bill now before us?
There will be the further complications to which the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has referred when the Department of National Revenue seeks to carry out subsection 8 of section 22 of the Financial Administration Act in terms of reporting all of this.
I think that at some stage of the bill, perhaps when we get into committee of the whole, the Minister of Finance should try to straighten this matter out for us and tell us what is happening with regard to taxation collected under items 440m and 440n of the Customs Tariff.
The main point which I am sure concerns all of us in this house, certainly all of us in

the opposition parties at this time, is that there is a provision before us, a bill dealing with so little change in the Customs Tariff at a time when we have another document, that has not been presented to us for discussion in any way, which makes many more changes.
I think it was an affront to the rights of parliament to pass the surcharge on imports order and the government, by bringing in this bill, gives us no opportunity to deal with all of the changes made in the Customs Tariff in the past few months. Therefore we hope that somewhere during the debate on this bill the minister will tell us where we stand, tell us what rates the surcharges have been imposed on, and so on. We hope that at sometime in this session of parliament, if it lasts long enough, we will have an opportunity to discuss the question as to whether or not the surcharge on imports order was itself a legal and valid order.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and the house went into committee thereon, Mr. Chown in the chair.
On clause 1-Schedule A amended.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

Mr. Chairman, perhaps the Minister of Finance, who was formerly minister of national revenue and the collector of taxes, will just indicate to the committee to what extent the records of the department, since June 24, comply in every respect where there has been a remission respecting an import worth more than $1,000 abatement which should be reported to parliament in the public accounts, as outlined in section 22 of the Financial Administration Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All I can say in reply to that question is that I am no longer minister of national revenue, but I am quite certain I do not have to assure the committee that the provisions of the Financial Administration Act are being complied with by the Department of National Revenue.

Could the minister say while he was minister of national revenue for quite a long time after June 24-and I am sure he intended to do his duty with his customary assiduity-that every remission that was worth more than $1,000 to the taxpayer was recorded separately for report to parliament as requested under the law?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, did I hear my hon. friend say "customary ambiguity"?
No, I said assiduity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Oh. I thought perhaps I should raise a question of privilege. I did not keep

a detailed record of every entry made during the time I was minister of national revenue, but I have no doubt whatever that the provisions of the act were being met with while I was the minister, and are now while my successor is minister, in accordance with the law.

The order in council of June 24 refers to what I call abatements or discounts under the general tariff. In debate last week I pointed out that the general tariff is scarcely ever used in this country. It is the third column of the schedule in the bill before us but I do not think, even with respect to trade with Russia, that we have used the general tariff. However in this devious device of the cabinet in June, when they thought they could bypass parliament, they said they would use the Financial Administration Act to discount or to rebate certain duties normally paid.
I want to ask the minister if he looked at this carefully when he was minister of national revenue? Now he is Minister of Finance. Can he assure the House of Commons that all customs entries involving a discount under the general tariff which amount to something beyond $1,000, are being kept in the records of the Department of National Revenue and will be duly reported to parliament in accordance with the statute, in the public accounts in subsequent years.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It would appear to me that obviously my hon. friend has a pipe line somewhere which correctly or incorrectly informed him that this has not been done. Otherwise he would not be pressing the question as he is. These are not remissions in the ordinary sense of the word. As my hon. friend knows, under order in council we imposed surcharges, some to the extent of 5 per cent, some to the extent of 10 per cent and some to the extent of 15 per cent. Presumably there are thousands of entries going through various ports in the country month in and month out, and I am not in the position to say that this could be done. I fact, I doubt very much if it has to be done, that there has to be a record kept of each entry showing whether it is $999.99 or whether it should be $1001. I doubt very much that that has to be done but I cannot assure the committee whether it is or is not being done.
There are no remissions under this bill whatsoever. The only two items to which the surcharge applies are aircraft and aircraft engines, and all we are asking to do in this bill is to postpone the application of the tariff. If we do not pass the bill these two items will incur a tariff charge of 15 per cent. That tariff has been suspended year in
Customs Tariff
and year out. The suspension would expire and we are seeking to extend it for another year. Those are the only items to which the surcharge applies. Other than that there is nothing in the bill except some medicines, some special preparations, et cetera, which are being made tariff free.
To get the answers to the questions my hon. friend is raising at the moment I suggest the proper place for him to raise them is on the estimates of the Minister of National Revenue or of the Minister of Finance, if he so desires, when I can answer him in detail. But I am not at the moment prepared to go any further than I did just now because, as I said, this has a very narrow application; we only have the two items which are subject to surcharge at all.

Mr. Chairman, usually the minister and I debate fairly cordially, but I must say I rise with some protest when he refers to anything in the nature of a pipe line. He knows that I have been on the opposition side of the house for five years while he has been minister, and he knows that I have bent backwards-
You are there because of a pipe line.

I have bent backwards socially, officially and in every other way to never discuss matters of this kind with his officials. I think that on reflection he will consider that to be true. I want to say that my information with respect to a technical matter such as the filling out of a B-l form comes from the business street; it does not come from government officials. I have, perhaps more than anybody in opposition in this house, tried to stay away from embarrassing the minister's officials or anybody associated with government in so far as information is concerned.
I say to the minister the act says that any remission beyond $1,000 entails an obligation on the part of the government to report to parliament. My information comes solely from a non-government source, an agency that deals constantly with the import of articles because of the commercial activities of the individuals concerned. I am told that there is nothing on the B-l import form to indicate the discount from general tariff down to the real and effective tariff which would relate to the obligation on the part of ministers of the crown, under parliamentary statute, to report a forsaking of duty beyond $1,000. I hope the minister will take my word for no consultation with his officials.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will.

Customs Tariff
I knew he would; and it is true. I have followed this practice for many years-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will take the hon. member's word for it.
-and I hope the minister will soon be on this opposition side of the house, when I would expect from him the same consideration with respect to officials of the crown.
You won't be there; you will be here.

I say-and I challenge the minister to deal with this-that the cabinet has abused this statute. They had no right to use the Financial Administration Act for the purposes for which they used it. This question is important because it involves $200 million in tax money. Parliament surely has charge of tax revenues and tax imposition. I challenge the minister-and he will not put me off-to deal with this question. I say that the administration has been careless. First of all, they should not have used this section. No lawyer would properly have told them it was appropriate generally across this land to import this way goods which might be worth, in remission of duty, more than $3,000 billions. I would imagine there would be dozens of such transactions a day, and these should be reported in the public accounts.
I say the executive went beyond what any layman without any legalistic attitudes would have said was proper when they used the Financial Administration Act and said that a general tariff act of this country, which had never been used in this way previously, would be the basis for this cabinet order. This is executive action going away beyond, during the parliamentary recess and particularly after the electorate had given them a very poor result, the power given under the statute. They have not brought this matter before parliament. I want to know whether or not all customs entries involving more than $1,000 in remission of duty, as contemplated by this section, are being recorded in the Department of National Revenue.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

Just before it carries, Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister if he knows of any commodities other than lobsters on which the government inadvertently put a surcharge on June 24; and if so, will he come clean and tell us what they are.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?
I asked a question, and surely I will be given an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I did not think my hon. friend wanted an answer to a ribald question like that. I do not admit for a minute that it was done inadvertently. I told him the other night that I did not know whether or not the surcharge applied; but that does not mean it was done inadvertently; because there are several thousand items and I am sure that even with the mutual respect the hon. member and I have for each other he would not expect me to have several thousand items in mind. I said that at the moment I did not know whether or not the surcharge applied. I certainly did not admit that it was done inadvertently. In any event, the surcharge has now been removed, and further than that the witness cannot go at the moment.

Mr. Chairman, if the minister did not do it inadvertently, he did it advertently, which is a great deal worse. That means that this minister from Nova Scotia, who was the minister of national revenue when these surcharges were put on, put a surtax on lobsters deliberately. He either did it inadvertently or deliberately. I was letting him off easily by saying he had done it inadvertently, but now we have been told that a Minister of National Revenue from Nova Scotia, a Minister of Forestry from New Brunswick and a Minister of Fisheries from Prince Edward Island were deliberately led by the ex-minister of finance to put a duty on lobsters. That is what the minister said.
Oh, oh.

That is precisely what the minister said. But it does illustrate, as I said earlier on second reading, that this hole-in-the-corner method of making tariffs in the secret of the cabinet is no way to legislate and no way to tax. All taxes should be brought before this house. When they are brought before this house and subject to public scrutiny, this kind of inadvertence, or deliberateness, or whatever it may be, is not likely to happen.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if my hon. friend wants to play games we can talk about this from now till ten o'clock. He speaks about what my colleague the former minister of finance did to me. He has also lectured this house very, very often on the doctrine of cabinet solidarity. Therefore, whether I knew about it or whether I did not could not matter less, because I am a member of the cabinet which imposed this surcharge and I accept full responsibility for that. There can be no question on that score whatsoever. My hon. friend has talked about various things which we should and should not do. I realize

this is a terrible thing, really, to impose taxes in this way; what we should do is make a speech on the radio.
That is what you did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We should tell the people overnight what the taxes are. If my hon. friend wants to debate this matter from now till ten o'clock, he can go ahead and debate it. But I just want to go back to the point of order, Mr. Chairman. We are dealing with clause 1-and I am not so sure that it has not carried-and that applies to certain tariff items. Whether or not surcharges are in effect, whether or not they are imposed properly, whether the Financial Administration Act was properly passed by the former government-because we had nothing to do with that act: we are simply dealing with sections brought forward by the government prior to 1957, and if it is unjust, if it is illegal, if it is improper, then we are acting under a statute which we found on the books-is not the matter under discussion. I suggest this is absolutely irrelevant. Now that we are in committee and have had this general discussion- about which some question could be raised, but I did not raise it-I suggest that we follow the relevant words of the clause. There is no application of the Financial Administration Act to this clause, and we are dealing only with the particular items before us.

I am glad to acknowledge the good nature of the minister. These are, indeed, very technical and detailed matters, and as we have, here, in one volume-it is a large one-the individual items of the Customs Tariff, perhaps we could depend upon the minister and his continued good nature if we wish to refer these matters in the future either to the public accounts committee, which is concerned about the $1,000 cash remission, or to the banking and commerce committee-I am thinking of the details of these items. The minister is assenting-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I cannot assent on behalf of the committee. The committee is master of its own fate in these matters. If it wishes to inquire further into this subject I shall, of course, co-operate.

speechtext: There are two questions I should like to ask with regard to items 440m and 440n. Would you like to deal with them now, Mr. Chairman, on clause 1, or would you like to deal with them on the schedule?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Deal with them, now, I think.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
These are items which are referred to in both the documents which have been mentioned.
Customs Tariff

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: I wonder if the minister, with his capacity for explaining things, his good nature, and all the rest of it, will tell us how things now stand with respect to duties upon the items which come under 440m and 440n? What rate of duty is being collected at the present time on these items?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The notes I have in front of me show there was a tariff imposed, I forget how many years ago, on aircraft and aircraft engines. Parliament in its wisdom has seen fit from time to time since then to suspend the application of this tariff. As a matter of fact, I see this suspension was first brought in in 1952. It has been brought forward every year-it would have expired on July 1, 1962-but the tariff has not been applied. My predecessor announced in his budget speech last April a resolution to extend the suspension for one more year. My understanding is that in view of the fact that he made such a statement on the night of the budget it was treated by the officials of the Department of National Revenue as an indication of what the law might be, and that duties have not been imposed on these goods since then. I am not absolutely certain about that, but I will make further inquiries and tell the hon. member definitely when we come to third reading. My understanding is that no duties have been imposed following the statement of my colleague. The budget resolutions indicated the changes which would become applicable, and I assume that the charges have not been made since then.
The surcharges?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, the tariff items themselves. This deals only with the tariffs. If this item was not included, the tariff would be effective as of now. We are asking the committee and the house to extend this exemption to July 1, 1963, that is, to continue it for another year. However, a surcharge of 5 per cent is applicable under the order in council to which the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River referred a while ago.

Customs Tariff
The surcharge is applicable, it is being imposed and it is being collected. If the committee and the house do not approve this provision then, of course, there will be a tariff charge imposed as well as the surcharge.
I may say that this extension has been asked for by the aircraft industry and by everyone representative of it. The imposition which this tariff would have imposed on the air carriers would have been substantial. As an indication of the amounts involved, let me say that imports in 1961 amounted to $98,100,000 in respect of aircraft and $44 million in respect of aircraft engines. I do not want to anticipate possible arguments, but it might be said: if you impose tariff duties you might safeguard Canadian industry and, in particular, one or two companies which, we read in the papers, are experiencing difficulty at this moment.
I can assure this committee that these companies themselves do not want this duty imposed. They have been operating under a system whereby a duty has never been imposed since 1952 and they have no desire to see one imposed now. All we are asking is that the imposition of duty should be postponed until July, 1963.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If the hon. member would look at 440m he would see the words "of types or sizes not made in Canada on and after July 1, 1963". These would be free under the British preferential tariff and subject to 15 per cent under the most favoured nation tariff after that date. Those are the governing words-"on and after July 1, 1963". Until the time this provision is approved by parliament it would read "on and after July 1, 1962". This provision is intended to postpone the imposition of this duty until July 1, 1963.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I think that explains it in part. It explains it in the case of those types

or sizes not made in Canada. But it does not do so with respect to types and sizes made in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There would be a duty in any case on those types and sizes made in Canada.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: My other question is this: if no duty is being collected under the Customs Tariff at the present time, how is it possible to collect this 5 per cent? As I read the surcharge on imports order, the 5 per cent is arrived at by applying the general tariff and then using the Financial Administration Act to reduce it to 5 per cent. Can the minister answer that one?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not wish to get involved in a philosophical legal argument which might have to be used before the Supreme Court of Canada. However, there is a difference between a tax being applicable and a tax being collected. The general tariff is applicable but under the order in council passed last spring, it was suspended, with the exception of 5 per cent. That is why we are collecting 5 per cent surcharge at this time. Tariffs are raised to the level of the general tariff, and then a percentage is exempted. As I say, it is a philosophical legal argument around which I am sure my hon. friend and I could revolve in our own rooms late at night or in a discussion before a court; but that is really the premise upon which it is based.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: It is hard to figure it out.

As I understand it, any exemption or privilege expired on July 1, 1962. We have not in Canada the type of thing which I understand is in effect in Great Britain. They have a statute, namely the provisional imposition of taxes act, something that binds some of the suggestions of the administration between the time they are announced at budget time and the time at which it is possible for parliament to adopt them. This privilege of free entry apparently expires in July. How does the minister rationalize a free entry on anything that occurred, shall we say from July 1, 1962, to the time that we pass it, the Senate passes it and it is approved by His Excellency?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As I told the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, I think that it has been the practice, that tariff resolutions become effective when the budget speech comes down. It is true that we have not the act to which my hon. friend referred but it has been a matter of practice and convention in this parliament for many years. In any event the practice which is being followed now with respect to it is exactly the same as that which has been followed throughout the

years. I shall be able to clear up any difficulty with that matter when we come to third reading tomorrow, or whenever it may be.

May I direct the minister's attention to item 237a and ask him for some information on this item, one part of which deals with uranium in the form of pigs, ingots, billets or bars. Under this item I know

and I believe this is no change in the situation-that under the most favoured nation tariff the entry of these commodities or these minerals is free. What I should like to ascertain of the minister is the free entry of a commodity of this kind when we produce so much more of it in Canada than we can consume and where uranium communities are, in an economic sense, languishing. Perhaps he could tell me how much has been imported under this free entry clause in the last year for which figures are available.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am advised that this item was brought into the tariff in 1954 and has been in the tariff since then. As my hon. friend points out, the purpose of this matter at the moment is to extend this until July 1, 1964. I do not profess to be an expert in this field or to know as much about it as does my hon. friend who has the problem in his own constituency, and who is more conversant with this matter than I am. However, I am told that this is because we were dealing with uranium metal and we are dealing with heavy water which is required by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, and it is essential for the type of nuclear power stations developed in Canada. Uranium metal is also used as a fuel for our research reactors. It is because of these two matters that this is being extended. It has been in the tariff since 1954 and we are now asking for an extension to 1964. The imports under this item for the year 1952 will be approximately $125,000.

I appreciate the minister's explanation. I, of course, can understand why, in the years 1954, 1955, 1956 and 1957 an item of this kind of free entry would cause no concern at all because at that time the problem was not the consumption of uranium but rather the production of uranium. The minister says now that the imports of this commodity are explained because it is a kind of uranium ingot and bar which is not manufactured, I take it, in this country and that therefore, in the development of nuclear power, it is required because it is not made in Canada. I take it that is the explanation, and that it cannot be made in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: At first glance I have some difficulty in connection with relevancy of this amendment.
May I say a word on it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I desire to have some argument on it from the hon. member.

I should be very happy to say a few words on relevancy. We have before us a bill which is described as an act

Customs Tariff
to amend the Customs Tariff. As indicated in the explanatory note the purpose of this bill is to implement the budget resolution relating to the Customs Tariff. Of course, that is not a quite accurate explanatory note as we have had no budget in this parliament. This note referred to something having to do with another parliament. The bill is to deal with a resolution without a budget. It seeks to make certain changes to the Customs Tariff. There have been other and much more substantial changes to the Customs Tariff by an order in council which is referred to in the amendment. What I am suggesting is that parliament in amending an act to amend the Customs Tariff should do a thorough job, and put in a provision that unless parliament has an opportunity before January 31, to continue or unless this house has an opportunity to continue this order in council by a resolution, the order in council should cease to have effect with all the orders made in amendment thereof.
By this amendment I am not seeking to reopen the decision made by the house last week that these surcharges should be stopped now. I am admitting that they exist. I am not in the amendment questioning their legal validity. I am not raising any point except that if they are continued up until January 31, they shall not continue beyond that date unless this parliament or this house has an opportunity to continue this order in council by resolution. I am not saying that the government is obliged to come with an act of parliament. After all, this House of Commons is supposed to have the right to tax. I am saying that the government should bring a resolution into this house and get the approval of the house for the continuance of such orders as may by that time be effective.
Since the bill is a bill to amend the Customs Tariff and since my proposed amendment relates to section 4 of the Customs Tariff and to measures which unquestionably do affect the application of the Customs Tariff, I suggest that it is completely within the ambit of the bill before us, and therefore is completely in order. It cannot be argued, of course, that this provision would in any way affect the balance of ways and means because it does not seek to amend anything that was ever done by any parliament. The balance of ways and means can only be established, as the minister well knows, in the House of Commons and anything done outside the House of Commons could not possibly be construed as affecting the balance of ways and means as presented to parliament. Therefore, on the basis of the only two grounds about which there might conceivably be the slightest question, that is, 
whether the amendment is relevant to the bill, the first one which I think is the more important and the second one that it does not disturb the balance of ways and means as presented in the previous parliament and never amended, it seems to me that the amendment is completely in order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I should like to say that in the committee stage section 4 cited by the hon. member is not before the committee. He also says that the amendment does not affect the balance of ways and means. At first glance it seems to me that he is definitely imposing a limitation and therefore indirectly affecting the balance of ways and means by introducing this date provision. I should also like to submit that the very question that has been brought up was disposed of on a supply motion. Not long ago the house voted on a supply motion and decided to keep the surcharges. Subsequently some have been removed. It is not within the power of any hon. member in the committee stage to place the limitations incorporated in a vote of the house on a supply motion not long ago.
I should also like to argue very briefly by analogy. I think what the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has said applies equally to something put forward in the committee stage not very long ago by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River when he said that simply because the executive effected an order in council that practically throws out the legislation that we have before us this evening. If this is applicable to the particular question we are discussing tonight, it would be applicable to any piece of legislation which was affected by order in council during a recess. I think I am arguing quite validly by analogy here. Just because the order in council in June, to which hon. members have referred tonight, affects this particular piece of what is to them dramatic legislation, does not make their argument any more valid.
Briefly, the four grounds I have cited are first that the balance of ways and means is being affected indirectly by the amendment the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has put before us. Second, the whole question was disposed of on a vote on a supply motion. Third, section 4 of the act cited by the hon. member is not before the committee at the present time. Fourth, there is the very general question which I argued by analogy, though I readily admit not too clearly. On these four grounds I would suggest that the amendment cannot be upheld.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to say something on two of the points raised by my parliamentary secretary. I suggest that this amendment affects the balance of ways and means very directly because if it should be carried then, as has been pointed out with dire prophecies of doom by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, a very substantial amount of money would be involved. To say in one breath that we are doing something which is illegal in taxing people to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars, and then for another hon. member to say in the next breath that this does not affect the balance of ways and means at all, is certainly an exercise in semantics of which even I did not think the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate was capable. That is the first point.
Second, and perhaps even more pertinent, is the fact that the proposed amendment deals with section 4. We are in committee, Mr. Chairman, and the doctrine of relevancy applies exactly. I suggest to you with all deference that section 4 is not before the committee and therefore section 4 is not before the committee for amendment.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, we from this side of the house do not wish to endorse, as is implied in the amendment now before us, what has been done in the past by this government.
To support this amendment would be in fact like admitting that what has been done in the past is all right, and that it should continue until January 31, 1963, and even beyond that date should the house approve it.

Mr. Chairman, we absolutely refuse to be a party to the austerity program the government adopted on the 24th of June. speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate for yielding the floor. He probably was wiser than he realized for he may want to say something after I have finished. I think everyone in the house knows of our deep concern in this party about order in council P.C. 1962-902. I think everyone knows that we feel that order was invalid, and this would seem to put us on the side of any motion or argument that tries to attack it in any way.
But I must say I am scandalized by the wording of the amendment that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has put forward and I hope, Mr. Chairman, that he will presently save you the trouble of ruling on it and will withdraw it. If he does not, I hope you will rule it out of order for the reasons I am going to suggest to you.
I am concerned now, not just about the substance of the austerity program, which the hon. member for Lapointe has raised. I am concerned about putting on our statute books what I think would be some pretty bad law. If this amendment were adopted it would declare that the order in council in question was valid up until now and, in fact, that it would be valid from now until January 31 next. The wording is that the validity be continued. I could not vote for a motion that implied that the order in council had any validity at all and I do not see how you can put such a motion to the house.
I am also scandalized by the suggestion that it would be in order to overcome an illegal action on the part of the executive, in order to overcome something that the executive did that it should not have done without recourse to parliament, by a resolution of one house of parliament.
I am curious as to how this was drafted. I am with my hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate in his concern in trying to bring out the action of the Conservative government in imposing this tax by order in council, but this motion does not do that. This motion asks that the house now assume that there was validity to an order in council most of us in this house do not believe was valid. Somewhere in Beauchesne-I have it right here, page 167, citation 199 states:
Any irregularity of any portion of a motion shall render the whole motion irregular.
I suggest the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has committed a gross irregularity in advancing a motion that validates an order in council as to the validity of which we are complaining and therefore this motion is irregular and should be so ruled.

I am really amazed, Mr. Chairman, to find members of the treasury benches applauding a statement that their

Customs Tariff
order in council is so completely invalid it should not have been put to the house. I suggest to hon. members that they should sometimes listen to the arguments they are applauding before they start applauding them. I am, of course, shocked that I should have scandalized the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre; this shocks me and pains me, sir, but it does not alter my opinion. My opinion is that, by the votes of certain other members of the house not in the official opposition, a decision of this house was made only last week that this order in council should be treated as valid and continued. If the other members of the majority of the house had voted with the Liberal party, this order in council would not be there to complain about. We have no blame for the fact that is still there.
As Your Honour pointed out, and as the Minister of Finance pointed out, this order in council is in fact being used to collect these imposts. We have maintained, and the house would not give us a verdict, that it was unconstitutional. This was not our fault, either. They would not give a verdict that it should be stopped, and that certainly was not our fault. We say, therefore, that at the earliest possible moment parliament should be allowed to decide whether or not this order would continue. If my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre is right that the majority do not want it to continue, I cannot see what he would be worried about because the moment this resolution would come before parliament, parliament would rule out as illegal this order in council and it would disappear. I agree with him completely that this order is unconstitutional.
It is my opinion, although I am not a judge of the supreme court yet, and therefore I cannot give a ruling-
Oh, oh.
-it is my opinion that it is also illegal. However, the attorney general of Canada says it is legal.
How do we know?

How do we know? We do not know. But we do know that taxes are being collected by the order in council without any approval of this house. I have sought to use the only remaining device that seemed to be open to get some opportunity for parliament, before too long, to pass upon this order. I would far rather put in a clause that the order in council be cancelled forthwith. I could not have done that because of the votes of hon. gentlemen at the far end of the chamber last week. They are the ones that prevented that. So, I was doing the next best thing. This order in council is in effect

and I want to see it before parliament as soon as we can get it before parliament. I thought this government, which was going to restore the rights of parliament, would be so anxious to get it before parliament they would have seized upon this amendment of mine as a sort of attempt at any rate to give a cloak of respectability to their contract.
Perhaps I might now be allowed to deal with the point made by the parliamentary secretary with which I am astonished the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, with that delicate sense of propriety he has, did not deal. The notion expressed by the parliamentary secretary-I notice not repeated by the minister who is perhaps a little wiser-that the order in council could affect the balance of ways and means is, I think, almost more outrageous than the original order in council. To suggest this amendment would be out of order because it would affect the $200 million that we say is being collected unconstitutionally and that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre says is being collected illegally, could possibly affect any balance of ways and means ever presented to parliament-I might say, sir, that is what Charles I lost his head about.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate seeks to amend the bill by adding the following clause after clause 2.
The provisions of order in council P.C. 1962-902 of June 24,	1962 and any amendment thereto
made under authority of section 4 of the Customs Tariff shall cease to have effect after January 31, 1963, unless the validity of such provisions has been specifically continued by a resolution of the House of Commons.
In my view, this is a substantive motion which would require the usual notice and has to do with an addition to the bill rather than an amendment to an existing clause. The hon. member seeks the addition of a completely new clause, possibly outside of the scope or extending the scope of the bill. This is obvious by reason of the wording. I am looking at May's sixteenth edition, page 554 where subsection (1) reads as follows:
An amendment is out of order if it is irrelevant to the subject matter or beyond the scope of the bill, or if it is irrelevant to the subject matter or beyond the scope of the clause under consideration. Amendments which are irrelevant to the clause under consideration should, as a general rule, if they are within the scope of the bill, be moved as new clauses.
Then, subsection (3) reads as follows:
An amendment must not be inconsistent with, or contrary to, the bill as so far agreed to by the committee-
I find the hon. member's amendment, to some extent, falls in that category.
-nor must it be inconsistent with a decision of the committee upon a former amendment.

For these reasons, I do not feel the amendment falls within the rules I have cited from May, in that it does tend to exceed the scope of the bill, I have to find that the amendment is out of order.

Title agreed to.
Bill reported.

Mr. Chairman, before the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) is allowed to withdraw his amendment, may I point out that the member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) had also suggested that an amount of $10 be required for farm loans of $5,000 and less, and that farmers be asked to pay $50 for loans over that amount. We, therefore, wish to support this amendment, and we hope that all together we can legislate, once and for all, for the happiness and greater prosperity of the farmers.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before making the few brief remarks I wish to make 27507-3-114
Farm Credit Act
on this amendment, I want to bring to the attention of the committee that we have here a demonstration of the value of an opposition in parliament. This matter was brought to the attention of the house originally by the hon. member for Assiniboia and by members of the party to which I belong and the matter was discussed. Although it appears on the surface to be not a large matter, it has been proved to be an important matter. I want to say that I am sure hon. members of all opposition parties are very pleased that the minister, on considering this amendment, has in principle accepted it, because he has introduced an amendment which covers in principle the points put forward by the members of opposition parties. As far as I, personally, am concerned, I think this raises a question which will require consideration by the Farm Credit Corporation. Everyone knows that I give the corporation full credit for what has been done in recent years since the act became effective.
I do not know how counsel are appointed, but there are unnecessary costs involved in the appointment of counsel who are located in unsuitable places. I shall illustrate it in this way. The counsel for the corporation in the Kootenays resides in Creston and the land registry office is in Nelson, a good many miles away. Farmers who are borrowing live possibly 150 miles to the north or northwest of Nelson. They write to Creston, and counsel in turn writes to the registry office. They write back to him and there is a delay. I am not putting all the blame on the counsel or on the lawyers involved, but I know from personal experience, having been concerned with some of these applications for loans, that delays do occur. I think that in order to speed up the service as much as possible, as well as to lower the costs of legal fees, a review of this aspect of the administration should be undertaken to make sure that counsel are appointed in the most suitable places. I gather that legal fees have been somewhat excessive in relation to the total amount of loans granted-somewhere over half a million dollars, if I heard correctly. As I say, various occasions upon which there has been delay have come to my notice and I judge the same situation exists in other parts of the country. I urge the minister to have this matter looked into because I think we could improve the service and lower the costs in this respect.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext:
We appreciate very much the amendment which has been brought in subsequent to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Assiniboia. The hon. member for Red Deer, as reported on page 603 of Hansard, did say we would like to see the fee

Farm Credit Act
eliminated. One of the reasons for asking that this be done is because we feel certain information is gathered as a result of the appraisals which is helpful to the Department of Agriculture. If this is worth anything at all to the department, surely it is worth that $10. As I say, we felt the fee should be eliminated entirely, but we are certainly thankful that the minister has been, I was about to say, thick enough of skin to come along and do this job for us. It must have taken a little bit of sand to come back here and make this reform, because the minister did not have to do so. We would like to thank him.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext:
I am glad to have this expression of appreciation on the part of hon. members. I think it would be useful if we were to have on record the financial difference between the various proposals which have been made. The hon. member for Cariboo would then understand that this was not such a difficult decision, after all, for me to make.
The estimated revenue from the present fee for 1961-62 is $295,950. Under the proposal we had in mind as put forward by the Farm Credit Corporation, revenue from this source would amount to $285,000. Under the proposal of the hon. member for Assini-boia this would have cost the farmer $329,000. The proposal just made would yield $325,000. So the difference between his proposal and mine is $4,000 less for the farmers. So it was not too big a decision to have made. I should like to thank the committee for the consideration they have given to this question. I like to get good ideas, and when I get them I use them as far as possible.

Amendment agreed to.
Clause as amended agreed to.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext: On clause 4, the minister will recall that at the resolution stage I asked whether it would be possible for a group insurance plan to be taken out. Could the minister inform us whether under the revisions he proposes it would be possible for farmers to take advantage of such a scheme?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext: This is one of the matters we have under discussion at the present time with the Farm Credit Corporation. Insurance policies have been available to borrowers under part III. We have been extending them to part II, but this amendment makes it clear we have the legal right to do so. The point the hon. member raises is under consideration and a decision will be made on it in a year or two.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext: This would apply not only to farmers taking out loans but to those who already have loans; it would apply to them, also?

maintopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext: I should like to urge the minister to give some consideration to the suggestion which has been made. A number of agencies, particularly co-operative agencies, are now setting up group insurance plans to insure a farmer's life for the amount which he is borrowing, or the amount outstanding at any given time. This means that in the event of his death before the loan has been repaid, his beneficiary will get the amount of the loan still outstanding by way of insurance to wipe out the indebtedness. This affords very good protection and if it were done in respect of a large group such as the one which comes under this legislation it could be provided at a very low cost. Even some of the smaller co-operatives have been able to do this at a cost of less than 1 per cent added to the charges. When a group as large as the Farm Credit Corporation is involved, even that cost could be reduced considerably. The plan could be optional or it might be mandatory. I see no reason why there could not be an optional provision so that any farmer would be able to pay a fraction of 1 per cent extra each year to insure himself so that in the event of his death his family would not be left with a burden of debt, but would get the land free of any encumbrance as far as the Farm Credit Corporation is concerned.

Clause agreed to.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY

maintopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY

What clause 7 has to do with is the supervision fee charged annually for supervising the loan. In the original clause we have noticed that the appraisal fee of 2 per cent of the amount of the loan, or $100, is

now being removed. Under the regulation what we have done is to put in an appraisal fee of $25, or rather a supervisory fee. We charge $25 for the supervision he gets under this loan.
